overview.title: Documentation
overview.lead: How the engine fits together, and how to install it.

blocks.text: This is the **IT Kamianets 3D Engine**. In conversation and in internal notes it is also called the **ITKP 3D Engine**, or **ITKP 3D** for short. All three names mean the same thing.

items.label: Start a game
items.text: clone a constructor’s starter repository, set up the project with an AI agent, and send engine changes back as pull requests.

items.label: Installation
items.text: Unity requirements, the install order, and a Package Manager URL for each package.

items.label: Architecture
items.text: the layers, the schemas, the game kit, and how character, camera and multiplayer fit together.

items.label: Examples
items.text: a first-person game from a starter repository, a multiplayer match, and a room scan, step by step.

items.label: Packages
items.text: one page per package, with what it includes and its roadmap.

items.label: Constructors
items.text: starting points for each camera style, each with a starter repository.

blocks.text: Every package in one file, for quick reading or for an AI agent choosing packages for a new game: [packages.md](https://3d.itkamianets.com/packages.md).

items: **Schemas** (5): `3d-scene-schema`, `3d-asset-schema`, `3d-network-schema`, `3d-save-schema`, `3d-inventory-schema`. Plain JSON, readable without Unity.
**Core** (6): `3d-unity-core`, `-scene`, `-input`, `-character`, `-assets`, `-audio`. What every 3D game in Unity needs.

**Game kit** (8): `3d-unity-ui`, `-save`, `-synth`, `-graybox`, `-shell`, `-account`, `-update`, `-net`. What a shipped game repeats: screens built in code, saves, generated sounds, scene-builder helpers, and the shared start screens, sign-in, self-update and online sessions.

**Specific** (10): `3d-unity-interaction`, `-spatial`, `-xr`, `-firebase`, `-assetra`, `-network`, `-combat`, `-feedback`, `-ai`, `-inventory`. Editing tools, devices, platforms, services, and game systems (combat, effects, enemy AI, items) that only some games need.
**Constructor** (6): the Character View camera, controls and template for first- and third-person games, VR controls for headsets, and the cameras of the Fixed View and Top-down constructors.

blocks.text: The engine targets Unity only for now. The schemas stay engine-independent, so other runtimes can be added later.
Source code lives in the [IT-Kamianets GitHub organization](https://github.com/IT-Kamianets).

start.title: Start a game
start.lead: Clone a constructor’s starter repository under your game’s name, and it becomes your game.

blocks.text: Pick the one that matches your game’s camera. Each has a starter repository in the IT-Kamianets organization:

items: `3d-constructor-character-view`: first and third person, like GTA V or Elden Ring.
`3d-constructor-top-down`: viewed from above, like Hades or Vampire Survivors.
`3d-constructor-isometric`: angled camera, like Baldur’s Gate 3 or Diablo IV.
`3d-constructor-side-view`: viewed from the side, like Hollow Knight or Dead Cells.
`3d-constructor-fixed-view`: cameras placed by the level, like Resident Evil or INSIDE.
`3d-constructor-free-view`: free strategic camera, like Civilization or Cities: Skylines.

blocks.text: Each starter’s AGENTS.md says what to build first for its style.

sections.title: 2. Clone it under your game’s name

blocks.text: The clone is your game’s own repository. Point it at a new repository of yours before the first push:

blocks.code:
cd <game-name>
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/<you>/<game-name>.git

blocks.text: A starter is an empty Unity project (Universal 3D template, Unity 6000.6) plus what every game needs from day one:

items: `Assets/`, `Packages/manifest.json` and `ProjectSettings/`: the empty project, with one scene and the URP settings
`AGENTS.md`: the guide for you and your AI agent: creating the project, packages to add, what to build first, the engine’s rules
`CLAUDE.md`: one line that points Claude Code to `AGENTS.md`
`README.md`: a short start for people
`.gitignore`: Unity’s standard set, editor and OS files, and `Packages/*` (except the manifest and lock file) so engine repos you clone in stay out of the game
`.gitattributes`: scenes and prefabs as text (Unity Smart Merge once configured), art and audio as binary, Git LFS ready to switch on
`LICENSE`: MIT
In Unity Hub choose Add, select your game’s folder and open it with Unity 6000.6. The first import takes a minute; `Library/` is rebuilt locally and never committed.
In Project Settings › Player, set Product Name and the application identifier (`com.itkamianets.<game>`).
The project has no project-wide input actions asset on purpose: all input comes from `3d-unity-input`.

blocks.text: Merge these dependencies into `Packages/manifest.json`, keeping your existing Unity dependencies. This minimal Character View stack includes the camera, controls, motor and input used by the current first- and third-person games.
Add scene JSON, imported assets, spatial audio or XR only when your game uses them. These are separate capabilities, not requirements for every game.

items: **Interface first, then gameplay.** Start with `<game>-menus` and `<game>-hud` for a playable loop, then `<game>-core`, `<game>-maps` and what your game is about.
**Name game packages `<game>-<part>`**, package id `com.itkamianets.<game>-<part>`.

Game packages live in their own repositories, cloned into `Packages/` like the engine ones, so several games can share one (several Temnorid games share Temnorid packages). While the game is young, keep them as folders with their own asmdef under `Assets/<Game>/`.
Scenes, prefabs that wire packages together, and build settings stay in the game; reusable code goes into packages.

blocks.text: Open the game’s folder in your agent and ask for what you want to build. The agent learns the rest from files, not from memory:

items: `AGENTS.md` in the repository: read automatically by Codex, Cursor, Copilot and others; Claude Code reads it through `CLAUDE.md`.
[packages.md](https://3d.itkamianets.com/packages.md): the package reference generated from this website catalog. Check source and installed revisions when upgrading.
[llms.txt](https://3d.itkamianets.com/llms.txt): a short index of these docs for AI tools.

blocks.text: If you only describe the game, for example a team arena like CS2 but with wizards, the agent can pick the constructor and the optional packages from packages.md.

The `3d-*` packages are shared by every game, so changes go back to them through a pull request, never as a copy inside your game. Clone the package into your game’s `Packages/` folder: Unity loads it there as an embedded package, in place of its git URL, and `.gitignore` keeps it out of the game’s history.

blocks.code:
<game-name>/                       your game
  Assets/ ProjectSettings/
  Packages/manifest.json           tracked: Unity packages and the engine packages by git URL
  Packages/3d-unity-character/     a cloned engine repo, git-ignored, used instead of its git URL
  AGENTS.md  README.md

items: Clone the package into `Packages/`: `git clone https://github.com/IT-Kamianets/3d-unity-character Packages/3d-unity-character`. Without write access to IT-Kamianets, fork it on GitHub first and clone your fork. Unity now uses this copy instead of the git URL; the manifest stays as it is.
Create a branch for the change.
Open a pull request to the package’s `master` branch. Keep game rules out of it: the change must make sense for every game.
After the merge, delete the clone (Unity goes back to the git URL) and pin the manifest to the new tag.

blocks.text: Embedded package clones are local working copies. Keep their repositories separate, and keep the game manifest and lock file tracked.
Maintainers release an engine package in five steps, in this order, so the tags, this catalog and the games never disagree:

items: Bump `version` in the package’s `package.json`, following semantic versioning, and raise the engine versions in its `dependencies` when it needs something new from them.
Add the release to `CHANGELOG.md`: a `## X.Y.Z` heading and one line per change, with **Breaking:** in front of anything a game has to change.
Commit to `master`, tag that commit `vX.Y.Z` (the same version as `package.json`) and push both: `git tag vX.Y.Z` then `git push origin master vX.Y.Z`.

Update this website’s catalog in [its repository](https://github.com/IT-Kamianets/3d.itkamianets.com): the package’s `version`, `tag`, texts and known limits in `src/data/catalog/packages.json`, their Ukrainian in `src/i18n/ua.json`, then run `npm run build`, which validates the catalog and regenerates packages.md.
Move the games to the new tag with the pin script below, open each game in Unity once, and commit its `Packages/manifest.json` and `Packages/packages-lock.json` together.

blocks.text: The pin script is `tools/engine/pin-packages.mjs` in this website’s repository (`npm run pin`). Run it from a clone that sits next to the games in one workspace folder. It pins every game’s engine packages to release tags in `manifest.json` and `packages-lock.json`, and adds the engine packages a pinned version needs that the game does not list yet. It needs git and network access to GitHub.

blocks.code:
npm run pin -- --workspace .. --latest                         # every engine package to its newest tag
npm run pin -- --workspace .. --pin com.itkamianets.3d-unity-save@0.2.0
npm run pin -- --workspace .. --latest --games <game-a>,<game-b> --dry-run

blocks.text: `--dry-run` shows what would change and writes nothing. Without `--games` it updates every folder whose manifest lists an engine package.

Pin each engine package to its release tag before you release the game. The package pages show the pinned URL; a package without a tag yet can be pinned to a full commit SHA. The pin script above moves a whole workspace at once.

installation.title: Installation
installation.lead: Start from a starter repository, or install packages one by one from Git.

items: Unity 6000.6
Git installed, so Unity can fetch packages by URL
For room scanning with `3d-unity-spatial`: the Meta XR MR Utility Kit (`com.meta.xr.mrutilitykit`)
For `3d-unity-firebase`: no Firebase SDK; it uses Firebase’s REST API with your project’s `google-services.json`

blocks.text: Recommended editor: Unity 6000.6.8f1. The engine packages and our games are built and tested on it, so using the same version keeps your project aligned with them. This is a suggestion, not a requirement: any Unity 6000.6 editor works, and a different version is at your own risk.
Without the Meta XR MR Utility Kit, `3d-unity-spatial` still compiles and reports that scanning is unavailable.

Each constructor has a starter repository: an empty Unity project with git settings and an AGENTS.md that walks you or your AI agent through adding the right packages and building the game. Clone the one for your camera style under your game name.
The whole flow, from choosing a constructor to sending engine changes back, is in [Start a game](https://3d.itkamianets.com/docs/start-a-game).

items: In Unity, open `Window › Package Manager`.
Choose `+ › Add package from git URL`.
Paste the URL of a package from the table below.

blocks.text: **Add dependencies first.** Unity resolves a package’s Unity dependencies (such as the Input System), but not other git packages. So add each engine package a package needs before it: every package page lists them under Dependencies.

Every package declares its engine dependencies in its `package.json` too, ready for a registry. With git URLs Unity still does not follow them, so the rule above stays until the registry below is live.
For Character View, use this dependency-complete starting point:

The URLs on the package pages and in these manifests are pinned to release tags (`#vX.Y.Z`), so a project gets exactly the released version. Keep the tag when you copy a URL: without it Unity follows `master`.

The engine packages are going to the [OpenUPM](https://openupm.com) registry. Once they are listed, add this scoped registry to `Packages/manifest.json` once, and Unity resolves every engine dependency by itself: you list only the packages you use, by version.
Coming soon: the listings are prepared but not published yet. Until then, install with the git URLs and their `#vX.Y.Z` tags, as above.

The current Unity games use `3d-unity-shell` for menus and lobby screens, `3d-unity-account` for sign-in, `3d-unity-update` for release updates and `3d-unity-net` for host-authoritative multiplayer. Add the shell with all its engine dependencies:

Before opening the shell, fill your own `ShellConfig` (title, wording, colours, places) and set your Firebase project with `GameAccount.Config = FirebaseConfig.Create(apiKey, projectId)`: the engine ships no project, so without one the game plays offline. Direct-address multiplayer and Unity Relay are separate connection options; online play requires your Unity Services configuration.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.lead: Layers that point one way, and data kept in engine-independent formats.

items: **Schemas** (`3d-*-schema`): JSON formats for scenes, assets, multiplayer sessions, saves and inventories. No engine.
**Unity packages** (`3d-unity-*`): core systems every game needs, a game kit for shipping one, and specific ones for editing, VR, room scans, Firebase, multiplayer, combat and inventory.

**Constructors** (`3d-constructor-<style>-*`, and the shared `3d-unity-fixed-camera` and `3d-unity-topdown-camera`): one per camera style. Each adds only its camera and controls (flat or VR) and a starter template.
**Game packages** (`<game>-*`, e.g. `game-arena-*`): the interface (menus, HUD) and the gameplay (rules, maps, content) of one game.

blocks.text: Each layer only uses the ones below it, so a fix in a package reaches every game built on it.

items: `3d-scene-schema`: **where** things are. Read and written by `3d-unity-scene`.
`3d-asset-schema`: **what** things are. Resolved by `3d-unity-assets`.
`3d-network-schema`: **what happens between players**. Spoken by the deprecated `3d-unity-network`; `3d-unity-net` uses its own small messages.
`3d-save-schema`: **what a game remembers**. The envelope of a save file, written and read by `3d-unity-save`.
`3d-inventory-schema`: **what is carried and stored**. Items and containers, used by `3d-unity-inventory`.

blocks.text: Unity is never the permanent owner of this data:

blocks.code: Scene Schema → Unity Scene → Scene Changes → Scene Schema

blocks.text: Audio has no schema of its own: sound files are assets, and sounds placed in the world belong to the scene.

Character View shares `3d-unity-character` between first- and third-person controls. Fixed-camera and overhead games can use their own movement or command systems; installing a camera does not provide those controls.

items: `3d-unity-input` turns any device into actions: move, look, jump.
`3d-unity-character` walks, runs, jumps and handles slopes, with no camera of its own.
The constructor’s controls make forward follow the camera; its camera follows the character.

`3d-unity-xr` and `3d-constructor-vr-controls` do the same for a headset: the headset and controllers become the same `CharacterCommand`, so a VR player, a phone player and a bot all use one motor and one network.

blocks.text: A game is one Unity project for Windows, Android, iOS and Meta Quest. Differences between devices live in `3d-unity-input` (keyboard and mouse, gamepad, touch, XR) and in the constructor’s controls; per-platform differences are settings and small `#if` blocks.
XR stays off in every build except the Quest one. Game code never touches an XR SDK: it asks `XRStatus.IsActive` and reads poses through `EngineInput`.

**Decision: use `3d-unity-net`.** It is the engine’s multiplayer package, and every current Unity game uses it. `3d-unity-network` is deprecated: no game uses it, it gets no new work, and new games should not start on it.

`3d-unity-net` is a host-authoritative session over Netcode for GameObjects, with a roster, named events, player poses and host-published entities, for games that build their scenes in code and have no prefabs to spawn. The host runs the game’s rules and checks; clients send requests and show what the host publishes.
`3d-unity-account` (or `3d-unity-firebase`) keeps accounts and stats between matches; `3d-unity-net` runs the match itself.
`3d-unity-network` (server-authoritative characters with prediction and reconciliation, and session messages in `3d-network-schema`) stays available only for code that already uses it.
A shipped game repeats the same work around its rules. The game kit holds it, so each game writes only what makes it different:

items: `3d-unity-shell`: the screens a family of games shares (splash, landing, sign-in, onboarding, lobby, top and bottom bars). A game describes itself in a `ShellConfig` (title, wording, colours, places), names the player through `ShellIdentity` and can translate every shell text through `ShellText`.

`3d-unity-account`: a guest or Google sign-in over Firebase’s REST API, remembered between runs, in the Firebase project the game names with `FirebaseConfig.Create`. Not being signed in is a normal state.
`3d-unity-update`: keeps the game on its newest GitHub release and installs it silently on Windows. Being offline is never an error.
`3d-unity-net`: a small host-authoritative session over Netcode for GameObjects for games that build their scenes in code: host or join by address or online code.
`3d-unity-save`: versioned local save files, written safely, with a kept backup of the previous save.
`3d-unity-ui`: screens built in code with plain uGUI, placed by anchors.
`3d-unity-synth`: sounds made in code from waves and noise, so no audio files are needed.
`3d-unity-graybox`: stable asset ids on primitives and the Editor helpers that build a first playable.

blocks.text: The shell depends on `3d-unity-account`, `3d-unity-update`, `3d-unity-net` and `3d-unity-ui`; the others stand alone.
Game code stays out of these packages: a family of games keeps its Firebase project, profiles and wording in a package of its own, outside this catalog.
The catalog graph includes engine assembly dependencies and the JSON contracts a package uses. JSON schemas are not Unity packages and are excluded from the generated installation manifests.

sections.title: Where a game keeps its models

blocks.text: Every game made with the engine keeps its shared models the same way, so any tool and any AI agent knows where to look and where to put a new one. This is a rule for all games, not a suggestion.

items: One GLB per asset id, at `Assets/Models/<group>/<name>.glb`. `<group>` and `<name>` are the two parts of the id: `props/bench` is `Assets/Models/props/bench.glb`.
An id is `group/name`, written with lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Once a game uses an id it never changes: the id is the slot, and the file is only what fills it.
`assetra.json` in the repository root lists every model of the game. `source.uri` is the GLB path above, and an entry without `source` is a placeholder waiting for a model.

Working files (reference images, a generator's raw output, Blender files) are not listed and do not go in `Assets/Models`. They live in `Art/Models/<group>/<name>/` at the repository root, outside Unity's `Assets` folder, so Unity never imports them.
To swap a model, overwrite the GLB at its path (or change `source.uri`) and send it on. A tool such as Assetra sees that the file differs, gives the slot the new file and drops the old version.
A model is in meters, with +Y up, +Z as the front and the pivot at the bottom center. Textures are embedded in the GLB, and a file is at most 7 MB.

blocks.text: A game can keep a file named `assetra.json` in its repository root. It is a normal `3d-asset-schema` library that lists the models the game needs, so the engine and outside tools read the same list. Following it is optional: Assetra (assetra.itkamianets.com) is a separate tool by another developer, and nothing in the engine depends on it.

items: The game owns the list. Each model is an asset with an `id`, `bounds`, a `placeholder` shape and color, and a `production` brief (`brief`, `budget`, `textureSize`) for whoever makes the model.
An asset without `source` is a placeholder waiting for a model. With `source` (a GLB path relative to the file) it is filled.
`3d-unity-assetra` syncs the file with an Assetra project: new entries appear there, and models filled there come back to the `source` path. It never removes entries or overwrites files on its own.
The project info lives in `metadata.properties.assetra` (`project`, `name`, `modelsDir`), which keeps the file valid against the schema.

blocks.text: A model starts as a slot in `assetra.json` and ends as a GLB that fills it. The steps below are the recommended way; the tools named in them are suggestions. A developer may use any image generator, any 3D generator, or model by hand, as long as the result fits the slot.

The slot comes first. Before any model exists, the game adds the asset to `assetra.json` (`3d-unity-graybox` does it from the tagged placeholders: Tools › ITKP › Models › Update assetra.json from Open Scenes) and plays with the placeholder in its place. Everything a maker needs is in the slot (`3d-asset-schema` 1.1.0), so every tool works from the same brief:

items: `id`: `group/name`, the slot's name and the model's path.
`bounds`: the size the model must fill, in meters, measured from the primitive that stands in for it today. Optimizing scales the model to fit it.
`placeholder`: the shape and color shown until the model exists.
`production.brief`: one line saying what the object is, written as a prompt, such as `orange and white striped road barrier`.

`production.budget` and `production.textureSize`: the most triangles and the largest texture side (256 to 4096) the model may use. `production.rigged` marks a character that needs a skeleton, and `production.generator` records the tool and job that made the raw model.

The library's `production.style` is one style phrase for the whole game, added after every brief so the models look like one set; `production.workDir` is where the working folders live (`Art/Models` by default).
Progress is not written down: a slot is `placeholder`, `reference`, `raw` or `done` depending on which files exist, so it cannot drift.

blocks.text: Each slot has one working folder, `Art/Models/<group>/<name>/` at the repository root: `reference.png` (the image the model is made from), `raw.glb` (the generator's output, untouched) and, if there is one, `<name>.blend`. The `itkp-models` command line from `3d-model-tools` (`npm install -g github:IT-Kamianets/3d-model-tools`) runs the steps that can be automated. Then:

items: Reference image. `itkp-models prompt <id>` prints the image prompt: the brief, the style, and one whole object, centered, from a three-quarter front view, on a plain light background, with no ground shadow and no text. Use any image model, for example OpenAI gpt-image, and save the result as `reference.png`. Reject bad images here: this is the cheapest step to redo.

3D model. Turn `reference.png` into a model with any tool. Meshy is the suggested one: install it with `npm install -g meshy-cli`, sign in once with `meshy auth login`, then `meshy make` builds a GLB from an image or a prompt (`--dry-run` shows the credit cost first; `meshy make --help` lists the options). Ask for the slot's budget as the polygon target, save the output untouched as `raw.glb`, and note the job in `production.generator`.

Optimize. `itkp-models optimize <id>` runs Blender headless: it turns the model by `--yaw` so its front is +Z, scales it to fit inside `bounds`, puts it on the slot floor at the slot center, reduces it to the budget, shrinks its textures, exports a GLB with embedded textures to `Assets/Models/<group>/<name>.glb` and sets `source.uri`. Any editor will do if the result passes the check.

Into the game. In Unity, Tools › ITKP › Models › Swap Placeholders for Models in Open Scenes (`3d-unity-graybox`) puts each model under its tag and switches the primitives off, so colliders and gameplay code stay as they were; scene builders call `ModelSwap.Apply(root)` at the end. GLB files need `com.unity.cloud.gltfast` in the project.
Into Assetra. Assetra reads `assetra.json` (or `3d-unity-assetra` syncs it), sees the new file and keeps it as the slot's current version.

blocks.text: Characters follow the same steps, but rigging, animations and the animator are separate work after step 3. `itkp-models check` measures every finished model against its slot and exits with an error, so it can run in CI. It fails a model that:

items: Is more than 5 percent bigger than `bounds` on any side, or fills less than 95 percent of it on every side.
Does not stand on the slot floor.
Has more triangles than `production.budget`, a texture bigger than `production.textureSize`, an external texture, or more than 7 MB.

blocks.text: It warns when a model is off center, uses Draco compression, or fills less than 70 percent of the slot along one side: its proportions differ from the slot, so check its front or the slot's bounds. And look at it next to its neighbors in the game, not only on its own.

items: Shared before specific: if more than one constructor could use it, it belongs in a `3d-unity-*` package.
Code that two games need lives in a package, not in either game: the game kit exists because every game had its own copy.
Dependencies point one way, down the layers.
Input only through `3d-unity-input`; no package reads devices directly.
No game rules in engine or constructor packages.
Schemas are the source of truth; engine models mirror them field by field.
Optional SDKs (Meta MRUK) never block compilation; Firebase needs no SDK, it uses REST.

examples.title: Examples
examples.lead: Games and workflows the packages are built for.

sections.title: A first-person game from the template

items: Clone `3d-constructor-character-view` under your game name and follow its AGENTS.md: open the included Unity project, add the engine packages, and make the player prefab.
Press Play: `3d-unity-character` walks, the camera follows in first person, and keyboard, gamepad or a Quest controller all work through `3d-unity-input`.
Switch to third person in the camera settings, or let players switch at runtime.
Add your own packages, interface first: `<game>-menus` and `<game>-hud`, then `<game>-core` and `<game>-maps`.

blocks.text: Arena uses Character View camera and controls with `3d-unity-net`, `3d-unity-combat`, `3d-unity-ai` and `3d-unity-feedback`. The shared shell handles menus and the lobby. Game rules and maps stay in the game project.

Use `NetSession.IsAuthority` for host or solo simulation, and publish entity state from the host. The schema replay examples belong to the deprecated `3d-unity-network`; they do not describe `3d-unity-net` traffic.

Escape and Detective use `3d-unity-fixed-camera`: assign `FixedViewCamera.Subject` and place `CameraShotVolume` boxes with shot anchors. Call `HoldBasis` while movement input is held to preserve direction across a camera cut.

Caravan Guard uses `3d-unity-topdown-camera`. `OverheadCamera` provides bounded panning and zoom; set `Focus` and `Bounds`, then call `Snap`. Selection, placement and character commands remain game code.

sections.title: From a room scan to a scene

items: `3d-unity-xr` triggers a scan from a controller button and shows progress in a HUD.
`3d-unity-spatial` reads the physical room and produces scene data.
`3d-unity-scene` converts it to a scene document that follows `3d-scene-schema`.
`3d-unity-firebase` uploads it, and `3d-unity-interaction` lets people rearrange the furniture later.

blocks.code: Room scan → SceneData → Scene JSON → Firebase

items: `3d-scene-schema`: `room-scan.example.json` and `corridor-scan.example.json`, two scenes sharing a coordinate frame
`3d-network-schema`: `arena-replay.example.json` (a full match) and `join-request.example.json`

blocks.text: Each example validates against its schema, so it doubles as a test fixture.

The Temnorid games are built on the same packages. Their scenes are mostly built in code from primitives and tagged with stable asset ids (`3d-unity-graybox`), and each starts from the shared shell (`3d-unity-shell`), so the menu, sign-in, updates and online play are the same everywhere.

items: Temnorid Craft, Dungeons, Conquest, Arena, Caravan Guard, Hippodrome and Legends: the first games, each with its own rules on top of the shell.
Temnorid Escape and Detective: short fixed-camera episodes on `3d-unity-fixed-camera`.
Temnorid Master: seven trades in one workshop, with generated sounds (`3d-unity-synth`) and a backed-up save (`3d-unity-save`).
